p: Wes's narrower aisle is on hold, and the 133 is still boxed in red on the HEARTH room whiteboard, waiting for a fix.
Jun's model now holds what HEARTH has to do and twenty one interfaces, each with two owners.
At the end of week eight Jun presented that list to Halo's working group himself, with Nadia in the chair beside him.
Tamarack's air rack, the one Pavel Ruzicka promised would drop right in, failed three of its four connections in the model: power, coolant and data.
Nadia's email to Pavel started with four words: it doesn't plug in.
Halo moved HEARTH's berthing to a pass in the dark, and the arm operator asked for nothing shiny near his target.
Amara Osei. Program manager. She signed the price and guards the margin.
Wes Harland. Chief engineer. He wants his aisle back.
Odette. Safety engineer. She wants the alarm heard through a curtain.
Callie. Nadia's sister in Pueblo, Rosie's mom. Nadia finally made the Sunday call.
Tiago Ferreira. Test lead. He said the air rack's row meant trouble.
Frank Brooks. Nadia's father. A retired lineman who texts in capitals.
New in this chapter: Tess Okonjo.

Once a month Amara Osei stood on a wooden shipping crate in the high bay and talked to the whole company. The crate had come with the factory. Somebody had stenciled CENTENNIAL LIGHTING on its side a long time ago, and it was the only thing in the building tall enough to stand on that wasn't on a work order.

On Monday of week ten about four hundred people stood around it in their jackets, because the heaters in the high bay didn't catch up until noon. A few of them were standing on Tiago's blue tape without noticing. Amara read the new hires first, every name, and waited for each one to wave.

Then she did the numbers. HEARTH was on budget. HEARTH was on schedule. Halo was happy. She said it plainly and stepped down, and people clapped the way people clap for good news at nine in the morning. She hadn't mentioned the rack. Pavel still hadn't written back.
She found Nadia by the coffee urn before the crowd had thinned. I've got a number in my head for what the egress fix costs, she said. Tell me yours is smaller.
I don't have one yet, Nadia said. That's what the trade is for.

Amara looked back at the crate. We bid a firm fixed price. I signed it. Every dollar this costs past the bid comes out of FRO, not Halo. She tipped her cup at the room, at the jackets heading back to their desks. If it eats the margin, I'm the one who gets back up on that box and tells them.
She went to her ten o'clock. Nadia stayed by the urn and looked down the outline on the floor, at the red X by the hatch, and then at the end of the tape where there wasn't one.
Colleen's Flight Notes: decide on purpose.
Three airplanes and a legal pad.

Colleen was buying an airplane. She'd borrowed one for two years and finally admitted it, and on Saturday she met Nadia at a hangar at the airport in Erie, where a broker had three used four seaters lined up nose to tail. She had a yellow legal pad. Down the left side she'd written what she cared about. Across the top were three tail numbers.
I already know which one I want, she said, and nodded at the oldest one, a taildragger with faded red trim. That's why I wrote the list first.

Decision management is the process for making a choice on purpose. You identify the alternatives, describe them, evaluate them in a structured way, and pick the one that does the program the most good. Any process can raise a decision: an analysis turns up a problem, a review asks a question, a risk needs handling. The work comes in three parts. Prepare: state the decision, who makes it, by when, and how. Analyze: set the criteria, gather the alternatives, and evaluate each one with data, much of it from system analysis. Make and manage: choose, record the choice with its rationale and assumptions, and tell the people and processes that depend on it. A trade study is the usual form this takes on a technical question.

Not every choice needs a trade study, and part of preparing is deciding how much method a decision deserves. A minor choice that's easy to reverse can be made quickly by the person closest to it. A choice that's costly to undo, touches safety, or commits the program for years gets the full treatment. A real decision also needs real alternatives. Comparing the design you already like against doing nothing isn't a trade. Go looking for at least one option you didn't think of first. And sometimes the best move is to hold off on choosing. Set based design keeps several options alive and narrows them only as analysis and tests rule some out. It costs more early, and it keeps the program from betting everything on one guess.

Every decision also needs a clear owner, the person or board with the authority to make it, named before the analysis starts. Analysts recommend. The owner decides, and signs the record. When nobody knows who owns a decision, it gets made by default, usually by whoever acts first.

How the exam asks it. Order wins on decision questions. Define the decision and the criteria, then evaluate, then choose. An answer that picks first and justifies after is the wrong one. Fit the effort to the stakes: a minor, reversible choice can be quick. Set based design keeps options open until evidence narrows them.

Two lines sat in a box at the top of Colleen's pad: useful load with full fuel for her and two passengers, and an annual inspection with no open airworthiness items. Those don't get scored, she said. An airplane that can't carry us isn't a low score. It's a no.

Criteria come in two kinds. Musts are thresholds, often taken straight from the requirements, and an alternative that fails one is screened out before anything is scored. Wants are what you trade, and each gets a weight that says how much it counts against the others. Set the weights before you score, with the stakeholders who own the concerns, and write down why. Weights chosen after the scores are visible drift toward whatever somebody already liked. Keep the criteria independent, so one concern isn't counted twice under two names. Then score each alternative on each want, on a common scale and from data where you can, multiply by the weight, and add. That's a weighted sum. A value function turns raw values like seconds or dollars into scores on the common scale, so the conversion is written down instead of guessed.

The weighted sum isn't the only tool. A Pugh matrix compares each alternative with a baseline, criterion by criterion, marking it better, the same, or worse. It's quick, and good for early screening when the numbers are soft. Multi attribute utility methods turn each criterion into a utility score and combine them, much like a weighted sum with more care about how value grows. Pairwise methods, such as the analytic hierarchy process, set the weights by comparing criteria two at a time. When the outcome is uncertain, a decision tree lays out each choice and the chances that follow it. The expected value of a path is each outcome times its probability, added up. A path that costs one million dollars for certain beats one that costs half a million with a 30 percent chance of two million more, because the second one's expected cost is 1.1 million.
The taildragger lost. It was cheap and beautiful and it had the worst useful load of the three. Good, Colleen said, and didn't sound like she meant it.

How the exam asks it. An option that fails a requirement threshold is out before scoring. Weights come from the stakeholders and are set before the alternatives are scored. A Pugh matrix compares against a baseline. Expected value is each outcome times its probability, added up.
Then she asked herself how much more she'd have to care about price for the taildragger to win, and worked it out in the margin.

That's sensitivity analysis: change the weights or scores across a reasonable range and watch whether the winner changes. If it holds, the decision is robust. If a small change flips it, the decision is close, and whoever makes it needs to know exactly which judgment it rests on.
I'd have to care about money twice as much as I do, she said. I might, in April. Not that much.

The scores come from system analysis, and on a module some of them come from simulation, which is digital engineering earning its keep: a model can run fifty layouts in the time it takes to tape one. A simulation is only worth its inputs. Anchor it to measured data, check it against a case you already know, match its detail to the question, and list what it leaves out.

Two ideas from the quality characteristics part of the handbook live inside most trades. Affordability asks whether the system's life cycle cost fits what the stakeholders can pay while it still meets their needs. Value engineering is a method for getting there: break an expensive alternative into the functions it performs, and look for a cheaper way to perform each one without giving up performance, reliability or safety. It cuts cost. It doesn't cut function.

Life cycle cost is the whole bill: development, production, operation and support, and disposal, over the system's entire life. On a system that works for fifteen years, running and supporting it can cost more than building it. Cost effectiveness weighs what a system delivers against that whole bill, so a design that costs more to build can still be the better buy if it saves crew time and spares every year it flies. Some programs set cost as a requirement from the start, often called design to cost, and trade performance inside it. And an honest cost estimate is a range, with its assumptions written down, not one number.

Structure is there partly to protect a decision from the people making it. People anchor on the first number they hear. They favor the option they drew. A room that agrees too fast can talk itself past a problem nobody wanted to raise. Written criteria, weights set before scoring, data in place of opinion, and dissent recorded instead of smoothed over all work against that. Colleen wrote her list first for the same reason.
How the exam asks it. Sensitivity analysis tests robustness. Value engineering keeps the function and lowers the cost. Removing the function is descoping, not value engineering.

A decision record holds the problem, the alternatives, the criteria and weights with their reasons, the scores and where each came from, the sensitivity results, the assumptions, who decided and when, and any dissent. Then the decision goes to work. It may change system requirements or add derived ones, traced to the decision. Design definition takes the chosen alternative and works out the detailed characteristics needed to build it. And a choice usually creates risks of its own, which go on the register with owners like any other risk. Measurement keeps the decision honest afterward. It starts from an information need, what the decision makers have to know, and picks measures that answer it, such as predicted egress time tracked against its threshold.

Here's the card for decision management. Its purpose is to give a structured, analytical basis for choosing among alternatives when a decision comes up. It takes in the decision to be made, from whichever process raised it, the stakeholders' concerns, the alternatives, and the data from system analysis. It puts out the decision management strategy, the decision itself, and the record with its alternatives, criteria, rationale and assumptions. Then the work it sets off goes out: changed or new requirements to system requirements definition, a direction to design definition, new risks to risk management, and updates to the plans. Planning, risk management, configuration management and the technical processes all pick those up.

A recorded decision can be reopened, and the record says when. If an assumption it rested on turns out wrong, if a new alternative appears, or if the criteria change, the decision comes back for another look instead of being defended out of habit. Programs keep a decision register so anyone can see what was decided, when, by whom, and on what basis.

Here's the card for measurement. Its purpose is to collect, analyze and report objective data and information, to support good management and show the quality of the products, services and processes. It takes in the decision makers' information needs and the data the project produces. It puts out the measurement strategy, the measures with their definitions, the collected and analyzed data, and measurement reports, kept on record so trends show. Project assessment and control uses them next to compare progress with the plan, and decision management and risk management use them to see whether a choice still holds.

Measurement runs in two steps. Preparing means finding the information needs and choosing and defining measures that answer them, down to how each one is counted. Performing means collecting the data, analyzing it, and reporting it to the people who asked, in time for them to use it. A measure that answers nobody's question is noise, however easy it is to count.

FRO had no one who could model smoke, so the program brought in a fire protection engineer on contract for the trade. Human resource management covers that too: acquiring the skills a project needs when the organization doesn't have them, as well as growing the ones it does.

Here's the card for human resource management. Its purpose is to give the organization the people it needs and keep their skills current, so projects get qualified people. It takes in what the projects and the portfolio say they'll need, which skills and how many people by when, and the skills the organization already has. It puts out qualified people for the projects, training and development to close the gaps, and a current record of the skills on hand. Project planning picks those up when it assigns roles, and portfolio management uses the skills record to see what the organization can take on.

The split with project planning is worth knowing. Human resource management supplies the people and grows them. Project planning decides which roles the project needs and who fills each one. Growing people takes years, not weeks, through rotations, mentoring, training and certification, so the organization plans for the skills its next projects will need, not only the ones this project is short.
On the walk back to the cars Nadia told Colleen about the crate. That's not a HEARTH question, Colleen said. That's a company question.

Portfolio management is how an organization decides which projects to start, keep funding, redirect or end, balanced against its strategy and what it can afford. HEARTH is most of FRO's portfolio. Amara's margin is what lets FRO bid the next job, and four hundred paychecks ride on that. The program chooses the fix. The portfolio has to carry it.

How the exam asks it. A decision feeds other processes: derived requirements to system requirements definition, the chosen alternative to design definition, new risks to risk management. Measures come from information needs, not from whatever is easy to count. Human resource management supplies and grows people; project planning assigns them to roles.
At two on Monday afternoon Wes, Amara, Tiago and Jun were in the HEARTH room under the boxed 133, and everyone already had an answer.

Move three and four up by the hatch, Wes said. Galley goes aft. Done. Amara wanted the cheapest thing that cleared 120 seconds. Tiago said a better hatch would do more than any wall. Jun had a sketch of the back of the module he hadn't shown anyone. What does Nadia do first?
A. Go with Wes's fix and have Jun start moving the quarters on paper today.
B. Ask Helen which fix Halo would rather live with, and start from that.
C. Have Wes and Amara each make their case, then compare the two fixes.
D. Write the decision on the board with who makes it and by when.

Nadia writes it across the top of the whiteboard: decide how HEARTH meets the egress times in the fire and the leak, scenarios E1 and E2. Amara decides, on Wes's recommendation, by Friday of week eleven. Under it go four options instead of two, because Tiago adds his hatch and Jun finally shows his sketch. Amara reads the date and nods.

That's the one. Decision management starts with preparing: state the decision, who makes it, by when, and how. Arguing about fixes before the question is written means each person is answering a different question.

By Tuesday there were four options on the board, each with a letter and a name. A, Wes's drawing as it stands, with a better emergency procedure. B, the faster hatch: a lower sill and two handholds, plus small layout changes. C, moving the quarters: the faster hatch again, with all four quarters moved forward and the galley and hygiene station moved aft. D, the second door. Halo's next node carries a docking port for a crew vehicle, and Halo's assembly plan could berth it at HEARTH's aft end instead of on the core module: HEARTH first, then the node, then the first crew. A second hatch there would put quarters three and four a few steps from a door, with a lifeboat past it.
Jun had started the criteria list. It had the 120 second limit on it, and cost, and mass, and crew comfort, and "Halo likes it," all in one column.
Four options are on the board for the egress trade. How should the criteria be set up?
A. Give each option one overall score for how well it meets the requirements.
B. Put every criterion into one weighted list, the 120 second limit included.
C. Make the scenario times musts that screen options out, then weight the rest.
D. Weight cost and schedule, and leave safety to the requirements already set.

Nadia splits the list in two, musts that screen an option out and wants that get weighed. Musts: E1 and E2 met from every bunk. Wants: egress margin, smoke on the escape path, cost, schedule and mass. "Halo likes it" gets crossed out, because Halo's view goes into the weights. Wes's drawing as it stands will have to clear 120 like everyone else.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Musts are thresholds, usually from requirements, that screen alternatives out. Wants are traded and weighted. Keeping them apart stops a cheap option from buying its way past a safety limit.
Decision three. Who sets the weights.

Wednesday the weights came up, and the room got louder. Helen, on the screen from Halo, wanted smoke on the escape path to count for half. Amara wanted cost at thirty percent. Odette wanted egress margin over everything and said so in one sentence. Wes said weights were a way to make a gut call look like math.
I've picked hatches for thirty years, he said. Show me the four and I'll tell you.

Amara didn't raise her voice. I closed a program office once, she said, at the end of my last tour. Twenty eight people. I handed out the letters myself, because I'd signed the budget. She was looking at the board, not at anyone. Thirty on cost isn't me not caring about the crew.
Three stakeholders want three different weights, and Wes wants none. How should Nadia handle it?
A. Score the options first, then set the weights once the numbers show a leaning.
B. Set the weights with Helen, Odette and Amara before anyone scores an option.
C. Skip the weights and let the room pick from the four options side by side.
D. Have each stakeholder set weights alone, then average them into one set.

Nadia gets Helen, Odette and Amara to set the weights before anyone scores an option. It takes an hour. They land on thirty for egress margin, thirty for smoke on the path, twenty for cost, ten for schedule and ten for mass. Amara argues for thirty on cost and loses, and asks for that in the record. Wes says it's still a gut call. Five of them, Odette says, written down.

Exactly right. Weights express how much each concern matters, so they come from the stakeholders who own those concerns, before any option is scored, with reasons recorded. Disagreement goes on the record too.
Wednesday night Nadia was at her kitchen table with Jun's spreadsheet when her phone lit up. Her sister, Callie. It was after ten, which meant nights.
You called. Don't make it a thing.
I'm not making it a thing, Nadia said.

You're making it a thing in your head. I can hear it. Her crew was up a pole near Avondale swapping a transformer. She had twenty minutes. Nadia asked how she knew they were safe up there. I know it's open at my switches. They test it before they touch it. When I climbed I did the same. Twice, with the right meter, where I'm touching. I got that in Dad's class.
Then I've got two meters and a crew that isn't stupid. The line went quiet a second. You do this. You call and then you check my work.
I got it at the dinner table, Nadia said.
Yeah. I know you did. Then, quicker: He wants to see your module. He won't ask. Give him a day or he'll never come. Nadia gave her Thursday of next week. Callie's radio went, and she was gone.
Nadia went back to the spreadsheet. Each option had one E2 time, and each had been worked out by the person who liked it. Wes's used the engineers' walking speed.
Tiago's used the slowest of Helen's trainers from week four.
The four E2 times were each worked out on different assumptions. How should Nadia compare them?
A. Run every option on the same trainer walk data and find what sets each total.
B. Average the owners' estimates into one figure for each of the four options.
C. Use each owner's own numbers, but mark on the chart where the assumptions differ.
D. Rerun all four options on the times of the fastest of Helen's three trainers.

Nadia reruns every option on the same trainer walk data. On one set of assumptions the answer jumps out. The hatch sets the time: first arrival, plus fifteen seconds for each person through, plus closing. Moving the quarters barely helps, because everyone still queues at one door. A faster hatch, eleven seconds a person, gets to 117, with the quarters moved or not. The second door, two people through each hatch, has both closed by 105. Tiago reads it over her shoulder Thursday morning. It was the door. It was always the door.

That's the one. System analysis gives decision makers data they can compare: the same assumptions for every alternative, stated, and the drivers of the result found. Here the driver is hatch throughput, which no wall move changes.
E2 was the leak. E1 was the fire, and fire needed smoke, which FRO had never modeled. Odette found a fire protection engineer she'd worked with before, and Amara signed her on for three weeks.

A model of people needed people to check it against, so on Thursday Helen sent her trainers back to walk the tape, and she sent one more person with them. Commander Tess Okonjo was a government astronaut on Halo's first crew, in Denver that week for suit fittings. She was tall, in a gray Halo fleece, and she shook hands with everyone in the high bay, the forklift driver included, before she asked where the bunks were.
Tiago turned the lights down. Jun had a stopwatch for each walker. They took turns in every bunk, four runs each, eyes shut until the alarm went.

On the first run Tess came out of quarter one and turned the wrong way. She went aft, toward the galley, stopped at the opening of quarter three and looked in, then did the same at four, at two empty squares of tape. Then she turned around and walked to the hatch. Jun's thumb hovered over his stopwatch and he looked at Nadia. Nadia shook her head. Let it run.
She did it on every run, from every bunk. From quarter four there was only one quarter left behind her, three, across the aisle, and she checked it anyway.
Afterward Jun showed them the sheet. Her line was the slowest on it every time, eight to eleven seconds behind the trainers.
Sorry, Tess said. She didn't sound it. I don't leave a module until I've counted to four.
Helen was at the edge of the tape, looking at the floor. She didn't say anything. Nadia thought about the note in Helen's wallet, and the man with earplugs who'd been the last one out.

By Friday Jun had the engineer's smoke model joined to his own crew model: a food warmer fire at the galley, smoke moving with the cabin air, and four people walking from their bunks at speeds Jun typed in from Thursday's sheet. On the screen they were four blue dots. It looked finished. She'd signed enough sheets to know what that was worth.
FRO has never modeled smoke before. What should Nadia do with Jun's new model?
A. Model every detail of the cabin, down to the cable trays, before running it.
B. Run it on the engineer's standard settings, the ones she uses on buildings.
C. Run it once on Wes's drawing and apply that smoke pattern to all four options.
D. Test the model against the trainer walks and a published galley fire test.

Jun reruns the trainer walks as a test. The dots land within two seconds of Tiago's stopwatch. The engineer checks the smoke against a published galley fire test and it tracks. Then they write the assumptions page, nine lines. The first one says the cabin is modeled as one open volume with the fans at nominal flow.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Simulation earns trust when it's anchored to measured data, checked against a known case, matched in detail to the question, and honest about what it leaves out. The assumptions page belongs in the decision record.
Monday of week eleven Jun ran E1 on every option and put Wes's drawing up first, as it stood, because it was the one they'd have to beat.

Jun's E1 run, a galley fire, on the current drawing. The alarm goes at zero, and the galley aisle is impassable at 70 seconds. Quarters one and two walk away from the galley to the hatch. Quarters three and four, as drawn, get past the galley at 61 seconds, a margin of 9. With the seat track on one side only, they're past at 52, a margin of 18. The run models the cabin as one open volume, with the fans at nominal flow.
The numbers came out clean, every row filled. She felt the small click she used to get from a green PASS, and let herself have it.

Wes was standing at the back. He didn't say anything. Jun's numbers were the averages of everyone's runs, and the trainers had varied by six seconds either way. Tess's line sat at the bottom of every sheet.
The E1 run puts Wes's drawing past the galley with nine seconds to spare. How should results be reported?
A. Report each option's average run, with a note that real crews will vary.
B. Report each margin with its spread, the slowest walker's runs included.
C. Hold every result until the engineer reruns it all at a finer resolution.
D. Report each option's best run, the one from the most practiced trainer.

Nadia has Jun report every margin with its spread, Tess's runs included. She's not following the procedure, Jun says. She's the commander, Nadia says. She's the one who'll be in there. With Tess in, the faster hatch's margin at the galley drops from eighteen seconds to twelve. The second door's hardly moves, because with it quarters three and four walk away from the galley. Jun writes the driver under each one. For the faster hatch it's walking speed past the fire. For the second door it's the hatch.
Exactly right. System analysis reports results with their uncertainty and the factors driving it, so the decision maker can see which options are close to a limit and why.

Tuesday morning there was a print on Nadia's chair, Wes's new drawing. Note eight now read SEAT TRACK ONE SIDE OF AISLE ONLY, and the aisle was back to the width of the tape. Wes had initialed it. In the rationale box for note eight, for the first time, he'd written one line: aisle first.
Clipped to it was a change request in his own block letters, with the rationale already filled in.
When she went to find him he was on the phone with structures. He held up one hand without turning around. Nine seconds, he said, to her or to the phone. Cargo never had to run.
Jun had the matrix up by ten, with Wednesday's weights.

Jun's weighted egress trade, scored out of ten. Egress margin and smoke on the path count thirty percent each, cost twenty, and schedule and mass ten each. Option A's screened out, at 133 seconds on E2.
The second door came out on top at seven. The faster hatch was five point six, and moving the quarters a tenth behind it. Amara looked at the bars for a while. Run it with cost at forty, she said.
Amara wants to see the ranking with cost weighted higher. What should Nadia do?
A. Run cost from twenty to forty percent and show her where it flips.
B. Rerun it with cost at forty, and show her both rankings side by side.
C. Keep the agreed weights and tell her a change would reopen the trade.
D. Report the agreed result only, and keep the cost flip out of the deck.

Nadia runs cost from twenty to forty percent, taking the extra weight from smoke. The second door holds with cost at thirty. Somewhere near thirty three, the faster hatch passes it. Nadia puts the crossing on one slide. Amara studies it. So it comes down to whether money is a third of this. Whether you and Halo agree it is, Nadia says. Her voice holds. Amara notices that too.

That's the one. Sensitivity analysis varies weights across a reasonable range and finds where the preferred option changes. Showing the crossover tells the decision maker exactly which judgment the choice rests on.
Decision eight. Same door, less money.
The second door came in at four point six million dollars and six weeks. Amara's reserve for all of development had been eleven million when she signed.
If it's the door, it's the door, she said on Wednesday. Make it cost less. Wes had already priced a custom berthing ring for the aft end and a new hatch to go in it.
The aft hatch option costs four point six million of an eleven million reserve. How should Nadia handle cost?
A. Save on the aft hatch with one latch in place of the forward hatch's two.
B. Leave cost alone until design is finished and the real numbers are known.
C. List the door's functions with Wes, then do each one cheaper, losing none.
D. Ask Wes for the cheapest aft hatch he can build, and take what it can do.

Nadia asks Wes and Jun for everything the second door has to do, one function at a time. They come up with five: open, pass a person, seal, hold pressure, berth. The aft hatch becomes a copy of the forward hatch, designed once and built twice. The custom ring becomes Halo's standard passive ring, which Halo already qualifies. The door drops to three point eight million. The crew lose nothing.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. Value engineering analyzes functions and finds the lowest life cycle cost way to perform each one, without lowering performance, reliability or safety. Affordability is the goal it serves.

Thursday her father, Frank, drove up from Pueblo and was in the lot at eight, because he'd left at six to beat traffic that wasn't there. He wore his work jacket zipped to the collar, though the high bay was warm by then.

Tiago met them at the door. Frank shook his hand with his right. His left stayed in his jacket pocket, and it stayed there the whole tour. She'd meant to show him the model. He wanted the tape. At the end of it he stood in quarter four's square a while, the left hand still in the pocket. That's the long way.
He looked at her instead of the tape, a beat past how he usually looked at anybody. Then they went out to the pressure test cell.
At the cell he stopped. Six red lockout tags hung on the valve panel, each with a name and a date. He read every one, bending for the ones down low.
I do, Tiago said. Then the person whose name is on it checks again. Only they take it off. Frank nodded and touched the nearest tag with his right hand, squaring it on its wire.
In the lot he said it was a clean shop. She waited for the rest of it. There wasn't any. After his truck was gone she went back in and read the six tags herself.
A text from Callie. He called me from the truck. Said clean shop. You know that's the top of his scale, right?

That afternoon Helen wrote that Halo would work toward berthing its node at HEARTH's aft end before the first crew moved in. Work toward. If it slipped, she wrote, Halo would fly three until it berthed, and she'd be the one who told the fourth.
Where does the second door's dependence on Halo's schedule belong?
A. Note it as an assumption in the trade record, to recheck at design review.
B. Take the door off the board and decide among the options that don't need the node.
C. Put it on HEARTH's register with Nadia as owner and Halo's plan as the trigger.
D. Leave it off HEARTH's register as a risk that belongs to Halo's node team.
Nadia puts the node on HEARTH's risk register with her own name on it. The trigger is Halo's next assembly plan not showing the node. Helen's fallback goes in as the contingency, signed.

Exactly right. Risk management identifies the risks a decision creates, analyzes them, and plans the handling: here, mitigation through a written commitment and a contingency with a trigger, all with an owner.
Amara would decide at nine on Friday. Thursday night the HEARTH room emptied out around Nadia until it was her, the 133 in its red box, and a blank decision record.
Wes stuck his head in on his way out. One page, he said. Nobody reads two.
Amara decides at nine on Friday, and the decision record is still blank. What should go in it?
A. Let the minutes from Friday's meeting serve as the record of the decision.
B. Write a record a stranger could check, with the reason for each number.
C. Record the decision and its final scores, with the whole matrix attached.
D. Record the winning option and its cost, with the rest kept in Jun's model.

Nadia writes it so a stranger could check every number. It runs a page and a half. The assumptions get their own block, nine lines from the model and one from Helen. Amara's thirty percent goes in under dissent with her name on it. Wes reads the first page and turns it over to see the half.

That's the one. A decision record captures what was decided and why: alternatives, criteria and weights with reasons, data and sources, sensitivity, assumptions, the decision maker, and dissent. It's what lets anyone check or revisit it later.
At nine on Friday Amara chose D, the second door, and signed the bottom of the page. She looked at the schedule line a while and didn't say anything about it.
Then she capped her pen. If I'm spending three point eight million on this, I want to know every week whether it's still working. What do I look at?
Amara has signed for the second door and wants a weekly view of it. What should Nadia give her?
A. Send her a weekly report with all the model and schedule can produce.
B. Track the percent of the door's design tasks finished each week against the plan.
C. Wait for the design reviews to show whether the fix is still working.
D. Find out what Amara needs to see each week, then pick measures for it.

Nadia asks what Amara needs to know each week before she picks a single measure. It comes to three things: is the crew still getting out in time, is the fix still on budget, and is Halo's node still coming. So, predicted E1 and E2 margins as technical performance measures against their thresholds, cost to complete on the second door, and the node risk's status. It fits on a card. Amara puts it in her pocket.

Good. That's the call I'd sign. The measurement process starts with the decision makers' information needs, then selects, collects, analyzes and reports measures that answer them. Fewer, better measures get used.
Friday afternoon Wes came by with a roll under his arm. He'd started the aft hatch from the forward hatch drawings, copied onto new sheets with AFT in the title block.
It's the front door with a new name, he said. I can have these out Monday.
Wes has copied the forward drawings onto sheets marked AFT. What should Nadia do?
A. Check the forward design against the aft hatch's own requirements and loads.
B. Hold the drawings until Halo's node team sends its complete interface design.
C. Use the forward drawings, and log the aft loads as an item to check at PDR.
D. Let Wes release the copied drawings Monday, with AFT in the title block.

Nadia won't take the copy on faith. Jun adds two derived requirements to the system set by change request, traced to the decision: the aft hatch's open time and its pass time. Wes checks the forward design against the aft end's loads and finds one bracket to thicken. The berthing interface with Halo's node goes on the interface list with two owners.

Exactly right. Design definition turns the chosen alternative into the detail needed to build it, consistent with its allocated requirements and interfaces. Reuse works when it's checked against the new conditions.

Amara didn't wait for the first Monday of the month. She called the company into the high bay on the Monday after, and four hundred people came back out in their jackets, curious, because she never called one out of turn.
Over the weekend Tiago had laid a second red X at the end of the blue tape, past the fourth bunk. People kept looking down at it on their way to the crate.
Amara climbed up with an index card. Nadia could see it from the urn. The top line was the one from week ten, HEARTH ON BUDGET, ON SCHEDULE, with a line through it.

HEARTH is going to be six weeks later than I told you, she said. And three point eight million dollars more than we bid for this piece of it. That comes out of us. I signed the price, so you're hearing it from me.

Then she told them why. She told it the way Helen had, from the bunks. Four people, one door, a hundred and thirty three seconds. The last one out is whoever sleeps in the fourth bunk. She pointed at the second X. People at the back had to turn around to see it.

Someone near the front asked how they'd decided. Amara held up one sheet, the decision record. Four options. Five things we cared about, weighted before anybody scored anything. It holds unless money is worth more than a third of this decision. I'm the one who signed the price, and I don't think it is.

Wes listened from the back of the outline, a step from the new X. Afterward he set his coffee on the concrete in the fourth bunk's square and walked to the X. Three steps. He paced it again to be sure, took his coffee and left.
Amara folded the card. I hate the six weeks, she said. I'd do it again. Both of those are true. Go back to work.
She stepped down. On her way past the urn she handed Nadia the card. Under the crossed out line, in the same pen, she'd written the new one: SIX WEEKS LATE. FOUR PEOPLE OUT.
